questions.topic: How a triangle constrains a figure group
questions.learningObjective: Identify the triangular composition of a pediment group
questions.stem: A brief for the pediment group asks that the three figures be arranged so the eye is led upward to a single head. Which compositional device does the brief describe?

options.text: A triangular arrangement, where the flanking figures lean inward and the central figure rises to the apex
A horizontal frieze, in which all three figures stand at the same height along the cornice
options.misconception: describes an evenly spread band rather than a triangle

options.text: A radial arrangement, in which the three figures face outward in three separate directions
options.misconception: turns the figures away from the centre of the group

options.text: A pyramidal arrangement, in which the central figure is hidden behind the two that stand before it
options.misconception: hides the apex figure instead of crowning it

questions.explanation: A triangular group closes on itself: the outer figures' gestures lead inward and upward to the apex figure, and the pediment's sloping sides frame it. A horizontal frieze spreads the eye sideways.
questions.hint: Think about where the eye is meant to end.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a dome needs at its base
questions.learningObjective: State the conditions a dome's base ring must satisfy

stimulus.body: A brief for a domed crossing states that the dome springs from a circular base of radius 7 m carried on a continuous ring of masonry. The note records that the base ring is 1.2 m deep in masonry, that its upper surface is level all the way round, and that any break in this ring would leave part of the dome unsupported. The architect asks what the brief should require of that base ring.

questions.stem: What must the brief require of the base ring under the dome?

options.text: That it be continuous and level, so the dome shell has an unbroken support all the way round
That it be thick enough to hold up the weight of the vault below, which presses down on it
options.misconception: confuses the ring with the support for a lower vault

options.text: That it be dressed with an ornamental band on the inner face where it can be seen from below
options.misconception: makes ornament the structural requirement

options.text: That it be built of a harder stone than the vault above, to resist the damp inside the building
options.misconception: makes stone durability the governing requirement

questions.explanation: A dome is a shell that works in compression and needs support all the way round its springing. An interruption in the ring leaves part of the shell unsupported and cracks open at those points.
questions.hint: Ask what happens if the ring is broken.

questions.topic: Two ways to set a dome over a square
questions.learningObjective: Contrast pendentives with squinches
questions.stem: Two schemes appear in the brief for covering the square crossing with a dome. Which statement correctly contrasts them?

options.text: Pendentives fill the corners with a single curved surface, while squinches close the corners with arches
Pendentives rest the dome on four columns, while squinches rest it on the four walls
options.misconception: confuses the two devices with their supports

options.text: Pendentives are used where the dome is small, and squinches only where the dome is large
options.misconception: ties the choice to the size of the dome

options.text: Pendentives and squinches are the same device under different names in different countries
options.misconception: denies that the two schemes differ

questions.explanation: A pendentive is a spherical triangle filling one corner and continuing the curve down to the wall, so the interior reads as one shell. A squinch is an arch across the corner, making an octagon.
questions.hint: Look at what fills each corner.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the drum under a dome buys
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purposes served by a drum beneath a dome
questions.stem: In a note to the client, explain what the drum beneath the dome of a crossing buys the design.

answer.exemplar: The drum does several things at once. It raises the dome clear of the roofs of the arms of the crossing, so the crowning lantern and the top of the dome read as a single object above everything else rather than being pinched in between them. It provides a continuous level circular base of constant height for the dome to spring from, which is what allows the shell to start without steps. Most importantly it opens a band of windows just below the springing, so the interior of the dome is lit from a source that is close to the light's final destination. It also collects the dome's outward thrust in a ring that can be taken down through the piers.

questions.explanation: The drum raises the dome above the roofs of the arms, gives it a level base and opens windows below the springing. It also gathers the thrust into a ring carried down by the piers.
questions.hint: Think about level, height and light.

Church A is a hall type, because its clerestory carries the light evenly across the whole interior

options.misconception: ignores the different vault supports

questions.explanation: Equal nave and aisle heights with compound piers is the hall type, where the vault descends to the floor and light reaches every bay. A clerestory above a low arcade is the basilica arrangement.

questions.explanation: A buttress works sideways, taking the horizontal push of a vault out of the wall it stands against. A pier works downwards, standing free and carrying the load to the ground.
questions.hint: Compare the direction of each load.

questions.topic: What a dome needs at its base
questions.learningObjective: Identify the thrust-resisting duty of a dome's base ring

stimulus.body: A brief for a domed crossing states that the dome is to spring from a continuous ring 1.2 m deep set on four massive piers. The note records that the ring is reinforced with a band of iron, that the inner face is to be finished with a ring of windows, and that the piers below are to be checked for the horizontal push delivered at the springing. The architect asks what the ring is for beyond carrying the weight of the shell above.

questions.stem: Beyond carrying the shell above, what does the brief require the base ring to do?

options.text: Resist the outward push of the dome at its springing, so the ring is not strained open
Provide a level surface for the masons to work from while the dome is built above
options.misconception: treats the ring as a working platform only

options.text: Hide the junction between the dome and the piers, so the transition appears to be a single surface
options.misconception: makes concealment the ring's duty

options.text: Reduce the weight of the shell above by carrying part of it down through the piers directly
options.misconception: misreads the ring as a load shortcut

questions.explanation: A dome pushes outwards at its springing, and the ring must resist that and pass it into the piers below. The iron band ties the ring together, and the windows are light for the interior.

With pendentives the four corners are cut away to a single continuous curve and the opening below the dome is 14.4 m. With squinches the corners are closed by arches and the opening is reduced to 11.2 m. What follows?

Pendentives give the smaller opening, and the continuous interior shell is a separate decorative treatment

options.misconception: reverses the openings and invents a vault ring

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the drum under a dome buys
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a drum is drawn as a separate element under a dome
questions.stem: In a letter to the client, explain why the drum is drawn as a separate cylinder rather than folded straight into the base of the dome.

answer.exemplar: Drawing the drum as a separate cylinder tells the reader three things that a single curved surface would hide. It fixes the height at which the dome springs, which is a structural decision, because the shell needs a level and continuous support at a constant height. It gives the architect a place to put a ring of windows just below the springing, which is where a domed space can most usefully be lit. And it separates the circle of the dome from the square of the crossing below, so the two geometries can be resolved in an orderly way. Making the transition look continuous is a matter of mouldings at the junction, not of merging the two forms into one.

questions.explanation: A separate cylinder fixes the springing height, gives a level base and provides the band of windows below the dome. Merging the two would leave the springing undefined and lose the window band.
questions.hint: Think about what a separate cylinder lets you show.

Flying buttresses replace the thick outer wall, and the cost is that the windows must be made much smaller

questions.explanation: A vault needs a wall that can react its outward thrust, unless it is braced. Flying buttresses brace it outside, but they land in the aisle, so the interior is divided.
questions.hint: Ask where the bracing has to stand.

questions.topic: Two ways to set a dome over a square
questions.learningObjective: Compare the interior effect of the two covering schemes

stimulus.body: A brief for a crossing offers two covering schemes to the client. In the first, the four corners of the square are each swept into a curved surface that runs unbroken from the wall to the dome, and the arches across the corners are omitted altogether. In the second, each corner is closed by a small arch whose crown carries a length of masonry across the corner, and a ring of smaller domes is proposed around the central one. The architect asks the client to weigh the difference between the two schemes.

questions.stem: Which difference between the two schemes in the brief is the important one?

options.text: The first gives one continuous shell with a large opening, and the second breaks the space into smaller bays
The first is cheaper because no corner work is needed, and the second is more expensive in labour only
options.misconception: reduces the choice to cost of labour

options.text: The first is only possible for a dome of small radius, and the second suits a large crossing
options.misconception: ties the scheme to the size of the dome

options.text: The first is structurally weaker at the corners, and the second distributes the load better
options.misconception: claims the swept corners carry the load less well

questions.explanation: With the corners swept into one curve the interior reads as one space under one dome. With squinches, masonry remains in the corners and the crossing reads as a central dome with subsidiary spaces.

It reduces the weight of the drum by replacing solid masonry with openings

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The structural difference between two churches
questions.learningObjective: Compare the load paths of a timber roof and a stone vault
questions.stem: In a design review of two schemes, explain how a timber roof and a stone vault differ in the way they carry their load to the ground.

answer.exemplar: A timber roof is light and works mainly in bending along its rafters, which bear on the walls and push outwards at the eaves as well as downwards. It needs a tie across the building to stop that spread, and the walls can be relatively light because the load is modest. A stone vault is very heavy and works in compression along a curve, so it needs thick piers, solid supports and a way to resist the outward thrust it generates. In exchange the vault is incombustible, it can carry a heavier roof load, and it can be pierced with windows high in the wall because the load is carried down in defined lines rather than spread along the whole wall.

questions.explanation: A timber roof is light and works in bending, spreading at the eaves, so it needs ties and light walls. A vault is heavy and works in compression, so it needs thick piers and support against outward thrust.
questions.hint: Compare bending with compression.

stimulus.body: A brief for a domed crossing sets out the two covering schemes in a table. Under the first, the corners are filled with curved surfaces that rise from the walls to the dome, the whole interior of the crossing being one continuous surface from wall to wall. Under the second, each corner carries an arch of its own, with a strip of masonry across the corner above it and a row of small domes on the piers between. The note records that the client has asked to be told which scheme gives the larger opening at the level of the crossing.

The second, because the arches in the corners are set further back and so open the space

options.misconception: denies that the scheme affects the opening

options.text: The first, because pendentives can be built at a shallower curve than the dome itself
options.misconception: invents a curve difference between the two schemes

questions.explanation: In the first scheme the whole corner is swept into the curve of the dome, so nothing stands in the way. In the second, masonry and arches remain in the corners and the openings are smaller.

questions.stem: A table compares two domes. The first springs at 4 m above the crossing floor with no windows in its base. The second springs at 11 m above the same floor and has a ring of sixteen windows just below its springing. What does the pair show?

The second dome is lit better but has lost the support that the first one has at its base
options.misconception: claims the higher springing removes the base support

options.misconception: assumes a low springing needs no drum

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a basilica plan is for
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of a basilica plan in a church
questions.stem: In a memo on the basilica plan for a new parish church, explain what the arrangement is for.

answer.exemplar: The basilica plan organises the church around a single axis that ends at the sanctuary. The congregation gathers in the central nave, and the aisles on either side carry circulation so that people can move to the front, to the side altars and to the doors without crossing the body of the church. The arcade between nave and aisles has a second purpose, because it is low enough to be roofed over, which allows a wall to be carried up above the aisle roofs and opened for windows. That high band is the main source of light for the nave, and it is the reason a basilica can feel open and tall while the ground plan stays simple and rectangular.

questions.explanation: The basilica plan gathers the congregation in a central nave, keeps circulation in the aisles and leads the eye along one axis to the sanctuary. Its low arcade also allows a clerestory above the aisle roofs.
questions.hint: Think about congregation, circulation and light.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The difference between a buttress and a pier
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a pier is not a buttress drawn differently
questions.stem: In an appendix on buttresses and piers, explain why a pier is not simply a buttress drawn differently.

answer.exemplar: A pier and a buttress are sometimes built of the same stone and sometimes join in the same mass of masonry, which is why the words get used loosely. The difference is in the work they do. A pier receives the weight of the vault above and passes it straight down to the ground, so it is strongest in compression and its size follows from the load. A buttress receives the horizontal push of a vault or arch and pushes back against it, so it is widest at the base and steps or slopes away above. A single mass of masonry can do both jobs at once, but the two functions still need to be distinguished when a design is set out, because they fix the size and the shape of the member in different ways.

questions.explanation: A pier takes the weight of the vault and passes it down, so it is sized by the vertical load. A buttress takes the horizontal push of a vault and pushes back, so it is widest at the base.
questions.hint: Compare the direction of the load in each.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The difference between a buttress and a pier
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a buttress from a pier in a drawing
questions.stem: In a note defining terms for the client, explain how to tell a buttress from a pier in a drawing.

answer.exemplar: Look first at where the member stands. A pier is free-standing on the inside, set in a line with the piers of the arcade, and it rises to receive the vault; in section it looks like a column or a cluster of shafts. A buttress stands outside the building, touching the wall only where the flying buttress lands on it, and it is stepped or sloping so that its mass is greatest where the thrust is applied. Follow the load as well: from a pier the force runs straight down into the foundations, while from a buttress it runs sideways into the wall it props. A single mass of masonry can do both jobs, in which case the drawing should say which part of it is doing which work.

questions.explanation: A pier is free-standing inside, receives the vault and carries it straight down. A buttress stands outside the wall, is stepped or sloping, and pushes back against the sideways thrust.
questions.hint: Look at position and at the direction of the load.

questions.topic: How a triangle constrains a figure group
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a triangular composition controls a figure group
questions.stem: In a commentary on the group in the pediment, explain how the triangle that the figures form helps the sculptor control the composition.

answer.exemplar: A triangle is the simplest shape that is stable in every direction, and a group arranged in one behaves the same way. The two outer figures give the group a wide base so it does not look as if it might topple, and the tallest element in the middle gives it a point to rise towards. That is also the shape the space itself imposes, because the field above a cornice narrows to an apex and leaves no room for a figure to stand tall at the edges. Working with the triangle rather than against it means the sculptor can use the full height of the field, since every figure sits where the space is generous and turns the eye inward.

questions.explanation: A triangle is stable in every direction, so the outer figures give the group a wide base and the central one a point to rise towards. The field narrows to an apex, so the shape works with the space.
questions.hint: Think about why a triangle stands and how the field narrows.

questions.topic: What the drum under a dome buys
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the moulding at the foot of a drum
questions.stem: A sketch of the drum shows the springing of the dome landing on a moulded cornice, with a second moulded band at the foot of the drum. What is the second band for?

options.text: It marks the line where the round drum meets the square of the crossing and closes the gap between them
It carries a band of sculpture around the base of the drum for visitors to read from below
options.misconception: makes the band a place for sculpture instead

options.text: It marks the height of the springing so that the masons can see where the shell begins
options.misconception: makes the band a setting out mark only

options.text: It collects the rainwater that runs off the dome and carries it down to the gutter above
options.misconception: makes the band a rainwater channel

questions.explanation: The drum is round and the space below square, so they do not meet on their own. The foot moulding closes the gap and makes the junction legible, and the cornice does the same at the top.
questions.hint: Ask about the difference between the two shapes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The structural difference between two churches
questions.learningObjective: Explain the loss of a clerestory in a hall type church

stimulus.body: A brief for a restoration compares the structural arrangement of two buildings in the same town. The first is a long hall with a high nave, lower aisles, a clerestory above the arcade and flying buttresses landing in the aisle. The second has no clerestory at all, its aisle and nave vaults springing at the same level from compound piers set inside the wall. The note records that the second building's vault is lit only by the windows in the aisle wall.

questions.stem: What structural difference between the two buildings does the brief record, and what follows from it for the second building's interior?

options.text: The second has no clerestory because its piers are inside the wall, so its light comes from the aisle windows alone
The second has no clerestory because its vault is a timber roof, so the light comes from the windows at the eaves
options.misconception: claims a timber roof for the second building

options.text: The first has a clerestory because its walls are solid, so the light has to be brought high into the nave
options.misconception: explains the clerestory by wall solidity

options.text: The second has no clerestory because its aisle windows are larger, so more light enters at a lower level
options.misconception: explains the missing clerestory by window size

questions.explanation: A clerestory is possible only where the nave is higher than the aisle and the arcade roofed. Where both vaults spring at one level there is no high band of wall, so the light comes from the aisle windows.
questions.hint: Ask where the clerestory could have been placed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The difference between a buttress and a pier
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the volume of a buttress mass
questions.stem: The brief specifies a mass of masonry for a buttress 2.4 m wide at the base, 3.0 m deep and 8.0 m tall. What is its volume in cubic metres?
questions.explanation: The volume is 2.4 x 3.0 x 8.0, which gives 57.6 cubic metres of masonry. Treating it as a wall of the same area but no depth would give 19.2.
questions.hint: Multiply width, depth and height.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a triangle constrains a figure group
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sculptor must consider the shape of the pediment field
questions.stem: In a written piece on the pediment, explain why the sculptor of a triangular group must think about the space as much as the figures.

answer.exemplar: The field above a cornice is not a rectangle that the sculptor fills, it is a triangle that narrows to an apex, and the space available at each height changes as the figures are placed. A standing figure needs a generous field around it, so the sculptor has to reserve the width of the cornice band for the figures at the base and build the inward turns of the drapery so that they do not foul the sloping sides of the field. Working with the triangle means every part of the group is placed where the space allows it, and the composition appears to fill the field without being crammed into it. A group that ignores the shape will either leave the upper corners conspicuously empty or have to be reduced to figures small enough to fit, and it will lose the focus that the narrowing field was going to provide for nothing.

questions.explanation: The field above the cornice narrows to an apex, so the space changes with height and a standing figure needs room around it. Turning the drapery to suit the triangle places each figure where the space allows.
questions.hint: Think about the shape of the field.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a basilica plan is for
questions.learningObjective: State the function of the aisles and the arcade
questions.stem: Two questions are raised in the design meeting: what the aisles of a basilica are for, and how the arcade's columns work.

options.text: The aisles take the circulation so the nave stays clear for the congregation, and the columns carry the arcade above
The aisles hold the secondary chapels, and the columns are only a screen with no load to carry
options.misconception: denies the columns a load path

options.text: The aisles collect the rain from the nave roof, and the columns divide the space into equal bays
options.misconception: makes the columns a decorative device only

options.text: The aisles light the nave, and the columns support a gallery running the length of the church
options.misconception: credits the aisles with lighting the nave

questions.explanation: The aisles are the working margins, carrying the congregation's movement so the nave stays free for the assembly. The arcade's columns carry the wall above the aisle roof.
questions.hint: Ask what each part of the plan is for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a dome needs at its base
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the volume of a hemispherical dome
questions.stem: The dome brief specifies a hemispherical dome of radius 7 m to be filled with rubble masonry of density 2200 kg per cubic metre. What is the volume of the hemisphere in cubic metres?
questions.explanation: The volume of a hemisphere is two thirds of pi r cubed, so 0.667 x 3.1416 x 343 gives 718.38 cubic metres. At 2200 kg per cubic metre that is 1580 tonnes of fill.
questions.hint: Use two thirds of pi r cubed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two ways to set a dome over a square
questions.learningObjective: State the consequences of the squinch scheme
questions.stem: A comparison in the brief sets out two ways of covering a square bay and asks which one the architect prefers. Which pair of consequences belongs to the squinch scheme?

options.text: The corners are closed by arches, which reduces the opening and breaks the interior into a ring of bays
The corners are cut away, which enlarges the opening and leaves the interior as a single continuous shell
options.misconception: gives the pendentive consequences to the squinch scheme

options.text: The corners are raised into a circle, which removes the need for any supporting ring at the springing
options.misconception: claims squinches remove the need for a base ring

options.text: The corners are filled with rubble, which reduces the weight the dome has to carry at its base
options.misconception: describes a fill rather than an arch in the corner

questions.explanation: A squinch closes each corner with an arch, so masonry remains there and the space below is smaller, the crossing reading as a central bay ringed by others. Cutting the corners away gives one continuous shell.
questions.hint: Ask what is left standing in the corner.
